orientation: The author is addressing Diognetus directly, beginning his critique of pagan idolatry by asking him to clear his mind and examine what the so-called gods really are.
pass_a_gloss: Come now, having cleansed yourself from all the reasonings that preoccupy your mind and having stripped off the habit that deceives you and having become as from the beginning a new man, since you are about to be a hearer also of a new word, just as you yourself also confessed: see not only with the eyes, but also with the understanding, of what substance or of what form they happen to be, whom you call and consider gods. Is not one a stone, like the one that is trodden underfoot, and is not another bronze, no better than the vessels forged for our use, and another wood, already even rotten, and another silver, needing a man to guard it, so that it may not be stolen, and another iron, destroyed by rust, and another clay, in no way more seemly than what is made for the most dishonorable service? Are not all these things of corruptible matter? Are they not forged by iron and fire? Did not one of them a stonecutter, another a bronzeworker, another a silversmith, another a potter shape? Before they were stamped into their form by the crafts of these human artisans, was not each of them, even still now, transformed by each of these? Could not the vessels that are now from the same matter become, if they should happen upon the same craftsmen, similar to such things? Could not these things again, the things now worshiped by you, become similar vessels by men, like the rest? Are they not all deaf? Not blind? Not soulless? Not without perception? Not immovable? Are they not all rotting? Are they not all being corrupted? These things you call gods? To these things you are enslaved? These things you worship, and you become completely like them. For this reason do you hate Christians, because they do not consider these things gods? For you, thinking and supposing that you honor them, do you not despise them much more? Do you not much more mock and insult them, worshiping the stone and clay ones unguarded, but shutting up the silver and golden ones and setting guards by night and by day, so that they may not be stolen? And as for the honors you think you offer them, if they perceive, you rather punish them; but if they are without perception, you worship them, refuting them with blood and fat. Let one of you endure these things, let someone endure these things happening to himself. But no man at all will willingly endure this punishment, for he has perception and reason; but the stone endures, for it is without perception. Do you not then refute its perception? Concerning the fact that Christians have not been enslaved to such gods, I would have many other things also to say; but if to someone not even these things should seem sufficient, I consider it superfluous also to say more.

choices.why: The author asks what the gods really are at the level of their material being; 'substance' preserves the philosophical force of the question.
The verb suggests removing a garment or burden; 'stripped off' keeps the vivid physical image of discarding the deceiving habit.
The compound verb with ἐξ- intensifies the likeness; 'completely like' conveys the full assimilation to lifeless idols.
The author uses the verb of cross-examination; 'refuting' captures the irony that their worship exposes the gods' lack of perception.
The term refers to the fatty smoke of sacrifice; 'fat' is the concrete sacrificial substance, keeping the sensory image.

pass_b_english: Come then. Cleanse yourself from all the thoughts that preoccupy your mind, strip off the habit that deceives you, and become like a new person from the beginning, since you are about to hear a new word, as you yourself have admitted. Look not only with your eyes but also with your understanding: what substance, what form do the beings you call and consider gods actually have?

Is not one of them stone, like what you walk on? Is not another bronze, no better than the vessels forged for our use? Is not another wood, already rotten? Is not another silver, needing a person to guard it so it will not be stolen? Is not another iron, destroyed by rust? Is not another clay, no more seemly than what is made for the most dishonorable service?

Are not all these things made of corruptible matter? Are they not forged by iron and fire? Did not a stonecutter shape one of them, a bronzeworker another, a silversmith another, a potter another? Before they were stamped into their present form by these craftsmen, was not each of them just like any other, and even now, could it not be transformed again? Could not the vessels now made from the same matter become like these, if the same craftsmen happened to work on them?

Could not these things you now worship be made by human hands into vessels like all the rest? Are they not all deaf? Blind? Lifeless? Without perception? Without motion? Are they not all subject to decay? Are they not all subject to corruption?
These you call gods? These you serve? These you worship, and you become completely like them.
Is this why you hate Christians, because they do not consider these to be gods?

For you who think and imagine that you honor them, do you not despise them far more? Do you not mock and insult them far more, when you worship the stone and clay ones without guarding them, but shut up the silver and gold ones and set guards over them night and day so they will not be stolen?

And as for the honors you think you offer them, if they have perception, you are rather punishing them; but if they have no perception, you are chastising them when you worship them with blood and fat.

Let one of you endure this. Let someone allow this to be done to himself. But no human being would willingly endure such punishment, because he has perception and reason. The stone endures it, because it has no perception. So do you not refute its lack of perception?
About the fact that Christians are not enslaved to such gods, I could say many other things as well. But if these arguments do not seem sufficient to someone, I consider it superfluous to say more.

problems.quote: was not each of them something else—and even now, could it not be transformed again?
problems.source_quote: ἦν ἕκαστον αὐτῶν ἑκάστῳ, ἔτι καὶ νῦν, μεταμεμορφωμένον
problems.why: Source says each was 'to each one, even now, transformed'; English 'something else' loses the distributive sense.
problems.fix: was not each of them just like any other—and even now, could it not be transformed again?
problems.ruling: Source: "ἦν ἕκαστον αὐτῶν ἑκάστῳ, ἔτι καὶ νῦν, μεταμεμορφωμένον" = ‘each of them was … even now transformed’; English adds ‘something else’ and a speculative question, altering meaning.

problems.quote: I consider it superfluous to say more.
problems.source_quote: περὶ μὲν οὖν τοῦ μὴ δεδουλῶσθαι Χριστιανοὺς τοιούτοις θεοῖς πολλὰ μὲν ἂν καὶ ἄλλα εἰπεῖν ἔχοιμι: εἰ δέ τινι μὴ δοκοίη κἂν ταῦτα ἱκανά, περισσὸν ἡγοῦμαι καὶ τὸ πλείω λέγειν.
problems.why: Greek says the author would say even more, not that it is superfluous. The sense is opposite.
problems.fix: I think I should say even more.
problems.ruling: περισσὸν ἡγοῦμαι καὶ τὸ πλείω λέγειν = 'I consider saying more superfluous'; English correctly captures this, not opposite.

problems.quote: Do they not all rot? Do they not all decay?
problems.source_quote: οὐ κωφὰ πάντα; οὐ τυφλά; οὐκ ἄψυχα; οὐκ ἀναίσθητα; οὐκ ἀκίνητα; οὐ πάντα σηπόμενα; οὐ πάντα φθειρόμενα;
problems.why: Greek lists 'σηπόμενα' (standing/immobile), not 'rot'; 'rot' is already covered by 'φθειρόμενα'.
problems.fix: Are they not all deaf? Blind? Lifeless? Insensible? Motionless? Standing? Decaying?
problems.ruling: σηπόμενα means 'rotting/decaying'; φθειρόμενα also 'perishing/decaying.' English renders both as 'rot/decay,' collapsing distinct Greek terms into redundancy.
